newsitem.title: UK: Oil price rises on U.S. gains, Iraq dispute.
newsitem.headline: Oil price rises on U.S. gains, Iraq dispute.

text.p: Oil prices ralled on Monday buoyed by technical gains in U.S. crude markets and concerns about Iraq's dispute with the Western powers that defeated it in the 1991 Gulf War.

A weekend U.N. Security Council resolution censuring Iraq for blocking arms inspections carried out under the terms of the cease-fire that ended the war over Kuwait gave oil markets jitters about the security of their supplies.
Benchmark Brent blend futures for August settled up 31 cents to $17.98 a barrel, lifted higher in a late rally spurred by gains on the New York Mercantile Exchange crude contract.

Iraq on Monday rejected as "unjustified" the United Nations resolution which threatened new sanctions and condemned Baghdad for preventing arms inspectors from entering three sensitive sites earlier this month.

While fresh sanctions will make little difference to already isolated and embargo-bound Iraq, the resolution casts a shadow over crude exports permitted under a U.N. deal that lets Baghdad sell oil to buy food and medicine, traders said.
The deal allowed Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of crude in the six months from December.

It was recently renewed but Iraq has held oil markets to ransom by refusing to clarify when it will restart exports. It has demanded $800 million still held in escrow accounts be released before it will resume supplying oil.

Iraq's nonchalance over the timing of its crude exports has unnerved crude markets and stopped the spiralling fall in oil prices from the $25 enjoyed at the end of last year to around $17 recently for a barrel of Brent.

The Iraq/U.N. dispute has also overshadowed this week's meeting of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) in Vienna, where the oil ministers of the 11-nation cartel hold bi-annual talks on their leaky production quota system.

Neither delegates nor independent analysts see much prospect of the cartel disciplining the quota busters who have pushed world oil prices down by pumping out two million barrels per day over the agreed 25.03 million bpd limit.
Most expect it will be too difficult to do other than roll-over the current output quotas.

"The ceiling is even more irrelevant that it was before and OPEC production will continue to increase in the second half of this year," said Geoff Pyne at Swiss bank UBS. "While oversupply persists prices will continue to fall."
With few surprises expected, the headline-hungry oil world will be looking to the Iraqi delegation in Vienna to make the news.
"Iraq has got people's attention by withholding supplies," said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at Smith Barney.
